what: Liquidia develops and sells treatments for pulmonary hypertension — dangerously high blood pressure in the arteries of the lungs. Its main product is an inhaled dry-powder form of treprostinil, delivered by a small handheld device rather than a nebuliser or an infusion pump.
customers: Pulmonary hypertension specialists and their patients in the United States, with the cost paid by insurers and Medicare.
money: Its inhaled dry-powder treprostinil product, launched recently.
moat: A dry-powder inhaler is genuinely easier for a breathless patient than a nebuliser that takes minutes per dose or an infusion pump worn continuously, and in a disease that makes breathing difficult, convenience affects whether patients keep taking the drug. The formulation and device are patent-protected, and the specialist prescriber base is small enough for a focused sales force to reach.
risks: A trailing net loss of $94.2M, and last year’s net margin was negative 43.5% — the company is spending heavily to launch.
The product competes directly with United Therapeutics, a far larger company that has dominated this disease for two decades and has litigated aggressively to defend it.
Revenue history is extremely short: $14.0M in 2024 to $158.3M in 2025, so there is no record of how the launch sustains.
The shares trade at about 8.2 times sales on a business with one principal product.
Eight analysts average a $66.13 target against a $56.63 price.
opportunities: Revenue grew from $14.0M in 2024 to $158.3M in 2025, with trailing revenue of $621.9M — a very fast launch.
Free cash flow of $291.2M is unexpected this early and suggests the launch economics are strong.
No debt reported, with $190.7M of cash, so the company is not dependent on financing.
A dry-powder inhaler is meaningfully more convenient than the alternatives in a disease where patients struggle to breathe.
Pulmonary hypertension is a chronic condition requiring lifelong treatment, so each patient started is long-lived revenue.
watch: Prescriptions written and patients on therapy. A single-product launch lives or dies on how many patients start and how many stay.
view: Liquidia is a single-product company in a disease dominated for two decades by one competitor, and both facts need to sit at the front of any assessment. United Therapeutics built pulmonary hypertension into a franchise, defended it through patents and litigation, and has considerably more resources. Liquidia’s answer is a better delivery device: a dry-powder inhaler instead of a nebuliser that takes minutes per dose or an infusion pump worn around the clock.

That answer is more substantial than it sounds. In a disease whose defining symptom is breathlessness, the practical burden of taking the medicine affects whether patients keep taking it. A patient who finds the regimen manageable stays on therapy; one who does not, stops. Convenience in chronic respiratory disease is a clinical variable, not a marketing one, and it is the honest basis of the product’s case.

The launch numbers are striking and should be treated with appropriate caution. Revenue went from $14 million to $158 million and then to $622 million trailing, with $291 million of free cash flow already — unusual this early and a sign the launch economics are genuinely strong. But a steep launch curve can reflect pent-up demand from patients and physicians who were waiting for an alternative, and the question is what the curve looks like once that cohort is through.

What makes this ownable rather than purely speculative is the balance sheet: no debt and $191 million of cash, so the company is not dependent on raising money at whatever price the market offers. At 8.2 times sales with a trailing loss, you are paying for the launch to continue. Prescriptions written and patients on therapy are the only numbers that answer it, and the litigation risk from a well-resourced incumbent is a permanent feature of this position rather than a passing one.
bull: A genuinely more convenient inhaled device keeps winning patients from infusion and nebuliser therapy in a chronic lifelong disease, funded without debt.
bear: The launch curve flattens once waiting patients are through, United Therapeutics defends with litigation and pricing, and a single-product company at 8 times sales has nowhere to hide.
